section_summary: This section concludes the pamphlet “America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt,” which argues that American steel, scrap iron, petroleum, machinery, aircraft, and credit were indispensable to Japan’s industrial expansion and war in China. The remaining documents consist chiefly of resolutions and appeals from churches, peace organizations, students, and China-aid committees seeking an embargo on war materials, followed by State Department replies explaining the limits and even-handed operation of the Neutrality Act. The correspondence also addresses civilian bombing, the proposed Peace Act, the Open Door in China, voluntary restrictions by exporters, and Central European refugees.

subfiles.title: America’s Share in Japan’s War Guilt
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression and contributing authors
subfiles.to: American public and Americans in China
subfiles.about: The pamphlet argues that American raw materials, machinery, petroleum, aircraft, and credit sustain Japan’s war in China and urges an embargo and organized public action.
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion of an earlier article explains Japan’s industrial-expansion program and its dependence upon American steel, oil, rolling mills, machine tools, railroad equipment, and cotton purchases. Eliot Janeway’s article emphasizes Japan’s reliance on uniquely American mass-production machinery, specialty steels, and lubricants, while excerpts associated with Byron N. Scott, Paul G. McManus, and T. A. Bisson argue that American exports directly bolster Japanese military operations. The final pages prescribe action by organizations, individuals, and Americans in China, describe the committee’s program and national board, solicit contributions, and provide an order form.

subfiles.title: Model letter urging action on House Resolution 527
subfiles.from: Unnamed constituent or organization
subfiles.to: Members of Congress and executive-branch leaders
subfiles.about: A model letter asks federal officials to end shipments and credits that support Japan’s war machine.
subfiles.summary: Model letter urges support for Representative O'Connell's Resolution 527 or other measures ending US exports of munitions, materials and credit to Japan.

subfiles.title: Shanghai circular supporting the Peace Act
subfiles.from: Unnamed American advocate in Shanghai
subfiles.about: The circular asks Americans to campaign for the Peace Act and end the contradiction between condemning Japan and supplying its military economy.
subfiles.summary: Shanghai circular says Japan gets munitions, oil and trucks from the US while American silk purchases supply exchange; a free China offers better trade; urges support for House Resolution 527.

subfiles.title: Summary of the Peace Act, H.J. 527
subfiles.from: Peace Act advocates
subfiles.about: A summary describes proposed presidential authority to identify aggressors and prohibit arms and other commerce with them.
subfiles.summary: Summary of the Peace Act, H.J. 527: the President would name an aggressor and make arms exports to it unlawful, with broader trade restrictions possible when necessary.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Washington Committee for Aid to China resolution
subfiles.from: Horace W. Truesdell, Washington Committee for Aid to China
subfiles.about: Truesdell forwards a resolution opposing shipments of materials for war purposes to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Washington Committee for Aid to China resolution, adopted by a hundred members at a November 29 dinner, opposes war-material shipments to Japan.
keywords: Washington Committee for Aid to China

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Horace W. Truesdell
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and provides arms-export licensing figures for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains a war finding would embargo arms to both China and Japan and no statutory authority exists otherwise; since July 1937 licenses total about $14.37 million for China and $10.79 million for Japan.

subfiles.title: Horace W. Truesdell’s follow-up on non-munitions exports
subfiles.from: Horace W. Truesdell
subfiles.about: Truesdell clarifies that his committee seeks restrictions on strategic commodities beyond items technically classified as munitions.
subfiles.summary: Truesdell says the committee focuses on scrap iron, copper, oil and trucks, not licensed munitions; advocates replacing the Neutrality Act and invoking Section 338 of the Tariff Act against Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Truesdell’s follow-up
subfiles.from: Joseph G. Green, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Truesdell’s recommendations for repealing and replacing the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Truesdell's December 21 letter and says his proposals will receive careful consideration.

subfiles.title: Methodist Board petition on American supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: George M. Bell, Board of Home Missions and Church Extension
subfiles.about: The Methodist board petitions the President and Congress to end American trade that supports Japan’s destruction of Chinese civilians.
subfiles.summary: Bell transmits a resolution unanimously adopted at the board’s November 17–19 annual meeting in Philadelphia. The resolution expresses shame that American aircraft, bombs, shells, scrap iron, oil, trucks, and other materials are aiding Japan. It asks the President and Congress to use every practical means to end the traffic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to George M. Bell
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the Methodist resolution and outlines the legal limits of the Neutrality Act and its policy on civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells George Bell a war proclamation would impose an equal embargo on China and Japan; no authority exists for non-arms commodities; the government condemned civilian bombing and told aircraft makers.

subfiles.title: California Progressives appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: H. Gale Atwater, California Progressives
subfiles.about: Atwater asks Roosevelt to stop American oil, gasoline, and munitions from supporting Japan’s killing of Chinese civilians.
subfiles.summary: Atwater argues the US can halt supplies used by Japan, claiming forty of forty-seven barrels of Japanese fuel oil are American; he favors restricting munitions and fuel, not broad boycotts.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to H. Gale Atwater
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds that invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo listed arms to China as well as Japan and could not restrict other commodities.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains the President's discretion not to proclaim war, that any proclamation would impose an equal embargo, and that the act gives no authority over other exports.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Ben Rice’s protest letter with clipping on J. Gordon Harrell
subfiles.from: Mrs. Ben Rice, Woman’s Missionary Society of Washington Street Methodist Church
subfiles.about: Rice protests American supplies to Japan and encloses a newspaper account of J. Gordon Harrell’s descriptions and predictions concerning the war in China.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Rice's protest letter with a clipping on Harrell's claims of civilian deaths and Chinese guerrilla resistance; he predicts Japan's finances will run out in six to eight months.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Ben Rice
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the Neutrality Act’s limitations and its condemnation of civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost's reply to Mrs. Rice: a war proclamation would embargo arms to both sides, no authority covers other commodities, and the government condemned civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: Federal Council of Churches appeal on voluntary discontinuance of war-supply sales
subfiles.from: Roswell P. Barnes, Federal Council of the Churches of Christ in America
subfiles.about: The council asks Hull to encourage voluntary termination of American sales of essential war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Federal Council of Churches statement condemns Japanese aggression and atrocities and urges aircraft, oil, truck and scrap iron suppliers to sacrifice profits; it seeks voluntary discontinuance with the Secretary of State's help.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Roswell P. Barnes
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department declines to extend its aircraft-export representations into a broader voluntary embargo on unlicensed commodities.
subfiles.summary: Moore says the approach to aircraft makers arose from civilian bombing, and a similar policy for all war-related articles is practically unenforceable since most commodities need no license.

subfiles.title: St. Olaf Student Body letter and resolution
subfiles.from: Winifred Hansen, St. Olaf Student Body
subfiles.about: St. Olaf students ask the President to halt exports and economic aid useful to Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: St. Olaf student body, about eleven hundred, condemns Japan's invasion and asks decisive steps against all war-useful exports and aid to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Winifred Hansen
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the student resolution and repeats its explanation of the Neutrality Act and licensed arms exports.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the resolution will receive appropriate consideration and encloses the Neutrality Act. He explains that a presidential war proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that the statute does not cover other commodities. The letter repeats the figures for licenses issued since July 1, 1937.

subfiles.title: Connecticut League of Nations Association resolutions
subfiles.from: Horace D. Taft and Florence L. C. Kitchelt, Connecticut League of Nations Association
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull and the U.S. Congress
subfiles.about: The association petitions against exports aiding Japan and endorses international cooperation to protect refugees from Germany and Central Europe.
subfiles.summary: Connecticut League of Nations Association resolution says US aircraft, scrap iron and oil make America complicit in destroying China; duplicates a resolution praising refuge efforts for persecuted Europeans.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Horace D. Taft
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges three Connecticut resolutions and explains its policy on the Neutrality Act, arms exports, and civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Moore's reply to Horace Taft: a war proclamation would impose an equal embargo, the law does not cover other commodities, and civilian bombing has been condemned.

subfiles.title: Church Council of Sacramento letter transmitting an embargo resolution
subfiles.from: John F. Woodard, Church Council of Sacramento
subfiles.about: Woodard transmits a resolution representing more than ten thousand Sacramento Protestants who seek an immediate end to war-material sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Church Council of Sacramento tells Roosevelt it adopted a resolution for immediate action against war-material sales to Japan.
